text: In the absence of further questions in the corporate matters and general questions section, we will now proceed to the next section. While I appreciate that many of the officials will remain for other sections in relation to corporate, we thank you for your attendance and answers.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We now move to outcome 1, which is 'Maintain a secure, reliable and affordable energy system; support the transition of Australia's economy to net zero emissions by 2050; support actions to promote adaptation and strengthen resilience of Australia's economy, society and environment; and take a leadership role internationally in responding to climate change'. Program 1.1 is 'Support reliable, secure and affordable energy'; and program 1.2 is 'Reduce Australia's greenhouse gas emissions'. Relevant officials are coming to the table. Senator Roberts, do you have questions on this outcome?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, I have questions on outcome 1.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: My questions are about the Tomago smelter power purchase agreement, which includes power from Snowy Hydro 2.0. The latest review of Snowy Hydro 2.0 shows that it will not be ready when the new electricity supply agreement for Tomago starts on 1 July 2029. The agreement includes a three-year transition that allows Tomago to access power from wherever they can find it, subsidised by the government. The question now becomes: where will they find it? Is anyone prepared to guarantee that the market will have enough firmed power to keep the smelter, the 1,000 mostly union jobs and the 5,000 indirect jobs alive in 2029? Is anyone willing to guarantee that?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
The Snowy 2.0 arrangement and the Tomago deal are entirely separate questions. If Mr Brine or his colleagues want to go to any detail on these questions, they will. Obviously, as you indicate, it's an important intervention, being one of the Commonwealth's interventions here to deliver and protect Australian industrial capability. In the Hunter, as you say, there are 1,000 direct jobs and 5,000 jobs that are utterly and completely related to that facility. It is important for the Hunter economy and Australian industrial capability. We are one of the few countries on earth that has an end-to-end aluminium supply chain, from bauxite to alumina and aluminium, through to finished products and advanced manufacturing products, including defence products, which engage aluminium.

It has been very clear from the operators of that facility that, for some years now, they needed new, clean and low-cost renewable energy. They were unable to secure that from the market themselves, and coal, or gas as a base load—rather than gas as a firming agent in the electricity mix—are, for them, far too expensive and in fact, the cause of their uncompetitiveness. This is a good, strong, capable facility. It's our youngest and largest aluminium smelter. But what was driving their lack of competitiveness was a reliance upon ageing coal infrastructure. They were very clear—privately, officially, informally and publicly, in every way that they could be—that what they required was new, clean energy capability.

We have worked with them and the government in New South Wales to deliver an outcome here that means more generation will be built and more transmission will be built that will deliver lower costs for the people of New South Wales and participants in the national electricity market, and it will deliver the security of that facility into the future. Essentially, in principle, it's just the same as the intervention in Central Queensland with the Boyne Island smelter, another really important part of Australia's industrial capability.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Renewables, solar and wind, cannot be firmed. I've asked about firmed power. The Central West Pumped Hydro Project near Bathurst has been cancelled, and, last week, the massive Alinta Oven Mountain Pumped Hydro Project was cancelled. Together, these total 1,225 megawatts of firming. So let me ask again: without pumped hydro, how will you firm the weather dependent power that you claim will be available to Tomago from 2029? So far, this government has no policy basis, no options evaluated, no cost-benefit analysis, no business case, no plan and no schedule. We're just going to drive off a cliff blindfolded. Where will you get your firmed power to save these jobs at Tomago that you have put in jeopardy?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Far from putting those jobs in jeopardy, the Albanese government has delivered a future for those jobs and investment in the Hunter Valley for more than a decade from this year, and that is investment as far as the eye can see.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Firmed power, please?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In terms of the electricity mix that is provided, it is firmed power. It may be that you are the expert and that the owners of the Tomago aluminium smelter don't know what they're doing! It could be. It is a theoretically possible position—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Real jobs are under threat, real threat, now.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: that you know all about it, and of the people in the army of engineering—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I know about the jobs that are under threat in the Hunter.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Let me finish. Maybe all the people in the firms that run this, including those in the electricity firms, as well as the trade unions that represent them, and the business organisations in the Hunter Valley know nothing and you know everything! That is theoretically possible.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Minister, the global manufacturing capacity—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Don't interrupt me.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I thought you had finished.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No, I have not finished. This is a serious deal—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It certainly is.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: put together by actual adults interested in the future of our industrial capability—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And I'm asking where the power is coming from. Solar and wind cannot be firmed. This is a gas—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senators, perhaps I can interpose here for a moment. Minister, please conclude your answer, and then I'll come back to Senator Roberts. Senator Roberts, I appreciate that you might not like the answer, but please refrain from interrupting at least while it's going on, and then we'll come back to you. Thank you very much.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The contracting for electricity—officials can go through that—will be from a multiple of generation sources. It will be the lowest-cost firmed capability for Australia.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What, specifically?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Don't interrupt me, please. We have the world's best wind and solar resources—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: They can't be firmed.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Please don't interrupt me. We have the world's best wind and solar resources, backed by gas and backed by storage. That is a firmed capability. Rio Tinto and the other owners of these facilities are very clear about what it is that they require. Absent delivering that, they will make their aluminium somewhere else. If we were to follow your plan and the plan of Mr Newman—I'm going to talk about hotel bills, Senator Henderson, and those specifically of Mr Newman—these jobs would go overseas. It is only practical action now that is delivering a real future and not a pretend future for those 6,000 jobs. That is the way that this government will approach it—practically and in cooperation with the states and territories, working with the firms that have responsibility for running these facilities and not on a magical mystery tour through what it is that uncredible sources say is the future of the electricity network—because we've got a responsibility to discharge on behalf of the country, the Hunter community and the workers and families that they support.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
You also vaguely mentioned gas as part of your answer. The global manufacturing capacity for large-scale gas turbines is controlled by just three companies: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. Those companies have their order books closed, as they're full, and have deliveries scheduled out to 2033. Whatever large-scale gas turbines we have on order now are all we are going to get for seven to 10 years. I note that Snowy's Kurri Gas Plant did get their generators in time from Mitsubishi. That gives you 650 to 725 megawatts of power for just 10 hours a day, except for one thing: the gas pipeline supplying the plant can only supply 70 terajoules of gas when full, which is only long enough for 10 hours of generation, and it takes longer than 24 hours to replenish or refill—basically, the pipeline is the storage—and demanding 'on demand' from other users in the Newcastle gas grid. This means that the people of Newcastle might find that they have a shortage of gas. Let's just set that aside.

Tomago needs 950 megawatt every hour, 24/7; in other words, it needs 22,800 megawatt hours daily. However, this gas gives you 7,000. Where are you getting the rest of the firmed electricity from for Tomago? There's no firmed power from solar and wind, and gas is giving you 7,000. Where is the rest coming from?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There will be a process—this is still under negotiation with Rio—where we transition to a fully renewable powered Tomago that will involve firming from batteries, gas and pumped hydro. The exact detail of those timeframes and the composition will be subject to commercial negotiations, but that's the plan at a high level. You would look at firming through batteries, gas and hydro. Snowy, of course, has Snowy 2.0, but it also has the ability to offer cap contracts into the markets under existing pumped hydro projects at the moment.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You've said 'batteries' and 'a process'. AGL Energy is building the AGL Tomago battery right next door to the smelter, offering 2,000 megawatt hours a day, provided it can source the weather dependent power, solar and wind, to replenish the battery. You are still well short of their needs, even if the sun and wind cooperate. Where is the rest coming from?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There will be a portfolio of assets drawn on. I think the Prime Minister has talked about three gigawatts of assets, and I expect that the majority of those would be in New South Wales. We see a number of wind projects coming through in the Central-West Orana REZ and the South West REZ. No doubt they will play a part and would be where the power is coming from. I draw your attention also to the Boyne smelter in Queensland. Rio were able to move to renewable-power that site by themselves, so what we're trying to do here is replicate in New South Wales what's being delivered in Queensland by Rio, by itself.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: For the record, the only way in which I can see this working is to keep all coal-fired power stations open and build at least one more new, clean-coal power station in the Hunter, which One Nation will do. Is there any admission yet that the only way forward for Tomago is more coal power?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: This is the problem. This is the One Nation 'close Tomago' plan. That's what that is. If you were in charge, there would be two sounds: firstly, that plan being announced and, secondly, that business exiting. Coal is too unreliable and too expensive because of its unreliability. The three companies that own that facility have been very clear about what they require from Australia's modernisation of its electricity capability. No matter how many times you say otherwise, wind and solar, backed by gas and other forms of storage—hydro and others, including batteries—are the cheapest forms of energy for households and industrial purposes—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Are you going to tell the people who are watching from home that is the reality?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: and that is precisely the case.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Where? Tell me of anywhere in the world.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No matter how much you and your colleagues try to mislead, people have far too much common sense for that. It's not an honest campaign, and it would have real practical consequences for 6,000 jobs in the Hunter Valley.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Exactly.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: They are good-quality jobs, and your position would destroy those jobs. It would close that facility, and it is a good facility that is worked in by people who are proud of their work for Tomago and for the country—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Six thousand jobs.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: and your plan would destroy those jobs. It's reckless about those jobs. Your objective is not to secure those jobs but to run a failing and negative political campaign that undermines Australia's energy security, our industry and our future resilience. You can keep asserting these kinds of propositions, as you have for years and years, as though you are the expert and all of these other people in industry, energy, engineering and economics don't know what they're talking about. It's possible, as I say—theoretically possible—that they all don't know what they're talking about and you do. I'll let other people be the judge of that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Fear does not replace facts. In summary, here are the numbers. You have 7,000 megawatt hours a day from gas, and you need a total of 22,800. Gas is baseload. You have another 2,000 megawatt hours a day from the battery, provided that the weather cooperates, and we've had solar and wind droughts in this country of four days or more. You have 43 from Snowy Hydro 2.0 at a rated capacity of 375,000 megawatt hours per annum production, and that's it. So far, you only have 9,043 megawatt hours out of the required 22,800 megawatt hours, which these 6,000 jobs depend on. Minister, how is the Tomago smelter power purchasing agreement not an exercise in pure fantasy—and that's being kind; I would use the word 'lie'—that will cost 6,000 jobs in the Hunter and decimate entire communities? Your government fabricated a story that's not truthful. Minister, if you are in power when the lights go out, you're finished.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
Instead of responding myself, I might just offer a response from the owner of the facility, who said:

As fossil fuels become increasingly expensive, this investment, combined with the power purchase agreements we have already signed, positions Boyne—

and that is in this case, but it is the same with Tomago—

to be among the world's first aluminium smelters underpinned by solar and wind power.

It also ensures heavy manufacturing like aluminium smelting can continue…

in this case, that is in Gladstone, but he makes the same comments—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: How? The numbers show that you're wrong.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Again, I'd just invoke the principle: the fewer the interruptions, the shorter the time that this takes. He continues that it 'preserves one of the few fully integrated aluminium value chains in the world'. I know, from observing your questions, that you find it impossible to conceive of how—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Numbers.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: and I understand that. You repeat numbers as though that somehow adds up to something real.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It doesn't, and that's the sad thing. Your numbers don't.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But there are people who have real money invested in this proposition—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: With taxpayer subsidies.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: and it's not pretend money but real money that sustains real jobs in a real industry, which needs to be supported by firmed, low-cost electricity.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But where is it coming from?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Mr Brine has explained to you where it's coming from—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: His numbers don't add up.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: and we will continue building while you continue undermining. That's our job. You stick to what you know best, but we are setting about the job of building a new electricity network for Australia because we take our future resilience seriously.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Snowy 2.0 is designated for peaking.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts, I will need to move the call on shortly. Do you have a final question?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I want everyone to remember the key number: 6,000 jobs are in jeopardy and there are no answers from the minister.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Why do you want to send them offshore?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you, Senator Roberts. Senator Smith.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I just want to turn to the most recent Australian Energy Ministers Meeting. Also, can you provide me with an update on plug-in solar?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The topic of plug-in solar was discussed at the recent Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council meeting on 11 September. Basically, it's the case at the moment that plug-in consumer energy resources are not legal in Australia, and that is because we currently don't have electrical safety standards that would allow them to be safely connected into people's houses. What happened at the September ECCMC meeting was ministers agreeing that officials should come back with advice on a way forward in terms of how we could have standards put in place in Australia, with a view to those devices becoming legalised and available to consumers to be used. That advice is to come back this year.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I've seen reported a 1 July 2027 date. What does that date refer to?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not familiar with that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It was in a Solar Citizens bulletin of sorts.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not familiar with that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Regarding plug-in solar, it says that states are expected to come back to the energy ministers council by the end of this year.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Commonwealth officials working with state and territory officials will come back with further advice to ministers on the way forward there.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So it's only the legality and the prohibition that currently exists that are being explored?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The main focus of the work initially is that, clearly, the question of legality needs to be addressed, if these devices are to be used safely in Australia. Potentially, there are a range of other issues that are relevant to the take-up of these devices, which are likely to warrant some attention in terms of other potential barriers that consumers may face. Again, we will be seeking to identify what those barriers might be and whether there are any actions that governments could be pursuing to alleviate them.

It has meant that there is increased daytime charging, lowering peak demand, and it has put downward pressure on wholesale electricity prices.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

text: I will answer your question. I would not characterise your questions in such a way. I always enjoy your questions. I don't find them tedious at all. For example, households with solar and battery storage used around 73 per cent less grid electricity during evening peak periods than households with solar alone. So there is an enormous benefit—dare I say a firming benefit, Senator Roberts—in the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. It is true that, because of the sharp fall in the cost of the technology—sharper than I think was predicted in the properly conservative design of the system at the outset—the parameters of the system had to be adjusted. That is true. That's what a responsible government does. But it is principally because the costs of the technology have fallen. That is a good thing. More Australians grabbing hold of this opportunity for themselves and for their country is a good thing—lowering costs not just for themselves but for their neighbours too. That is a very Australian thing to do. This is part of building a future Australia that's stronger and more resilient, with a lower-cost electricity system.

text: I will go to Senator Hodgins-May, but before I do, can I just indicate that we're now in a position to release the officials from the Emissions Reduction Assurance Committee from today's program. Senator Hodgins-May.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Minister Ayres, in May estimates you confirmed that data centres would have to produce additional renewable energy, not just cover their own load, about which we were quite complimentary. But on 5 August Minister Bowen said it was a causer-pays system where data centres only had to cover their costs on the grid. Then on 26 August the Prime Minister changed the policy so that coal and gas could power data centres. Then, the next day, the energy minister said, no, only after the Australian Energy Regulator has approved that coal and gas are cheaper than renewables. So what is the policy that will be presented in the legislation?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The legislation that hits the parliament will, on the energy questions, be designed to achieve a number of objectives. The most important objective here is that while data centres themselves are important bits of national infrastructure—just the same as a bridge or a road—everybody here who checked their phone before they got out of bed this morning would have engaged the services of at least one, if not more, data centres—everybody who has posted a meme or asked a question. I make the point that it's important infrastructure. For large data centres—and there will be more investment in those pieces of infrastructure—this legislation will use national rules to make sure that those investments don't push up the price of electricity, which is what has happened in other jurisdictions. A lack of planning and a regulatory framework has meant that there are more customers for the same amount of electricity generation and transmission infrastructure. Firstly, lower costs; that's what it's designed to do. Secondly, ensure that data centres procure new renewable generation, adequate firming, demand flexibility in terms of their own operations. Just the same as Senator Roberts and I were talking about the Tomago aluminium facility, it is required to have the capacity to be able to flex its demand to give the grid more stable capacity. So there are a number of objectives.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Is your answer different from your main answer, that they would be required to produce additional renewable energy, not just to cover their load?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You stand by that?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There will be a requirement, as I just said, to procure new renewable generation. Of course, there is a requirement for firming there too. Gas and hydro and other things play a role in firming in our electricity network. But the principle here is that large data centres bring their own electricity and that supports the development of the electricity network and produces lower costs rather than higher costs, which would be the outcome if we don't legislate a framework to require that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Will data centres be able to be built and connected before associated renewables have been built?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: These matters are, of course, the subject of the government's deliberations in the lead-up to new legislation being introduced, as the Prime Minister has indicated, shortly to the parliament. There's a range of proposals on duration and firming. We will be very transparent. There is a parliamentary process that's engaged about those issues now. The legislation will arrive in the parliament—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Is this something perhaps the departmental officials can enlighten us on further?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Questions around the transition arrangements will be dealt with very adequately then. If officials have got anything that they can add, I'm very happy for them to do that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: They're under consideration by cabinet at the moment, in the context of the legislation that the minister mentioned.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So we can't rule out that data centres will be built before renewables have been built?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We're in the middle of cabinet deliberations on those questions. It's not a secret; we have been very clear about these, and we've been engaging across the parliament on these questions as well. As you indicate, there are important principles involved here, and we want to see this deliver lower cost and help build out a modern electricity network.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There is significant community concern, as I'm sure you're very well aware, that if data centres can be connected before then we will see households and businesses pay extra costs, and it will put upward pressure on prices. Is the government assuring us that there will be nothing in this data centre scale-up that will stop bills going down?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Everything in the design of the regulatory framework that we bring to the parliament will be about delivering precisely that. As you would know, we came to government in 2022 against a backdrop of no investment in the electricity network. The principle here—not just in data centre terms but in industrial electricity terms and household electrification—is that all of the objectives that we want, to grow the economy, to reindustrialise the economy and to make the economy more efficient and productive, require more electricity. Yes, data centres are big users of electricity, but they are not the only ones. We've just spent some time traversing what has been going on in the smelting sector, for example, where low-cost electricity is really important. We have to build and build in order to meet those objectives in the electricity network, and there will be data centres that are required for our national economic development and for our resilience that will be large users of electricity. This policy is designed to make sure that they pay their own way.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: If Queensland can use coal and gas for data centres, will this lift prices for everyone on the east coast or just Queensland energy users? That's open to the department as well.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The way Minister Bowen has articulated what was discussed at National Cabinet is as follows. For a data centre to qualify for the exemption, data centres will be required to surrender REGO certificates to offset their demand, but if they procure power from a state-owned electricity provider, in a state that is predominantly a state-owned system, they can apply to the AER, the Australian Energy Regulator, to seek an exemption from that requirement. To be granted that exemption, they have to demonstrate that contract has benefits overall for system reliability and that it's cheaper for consumers overall. It's not that the data centre itself gets cheaper prices; it has to be cheaper for consumers overall. If they can't meet that requirement, then they would still have to surrender the renewable energy certificates.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
witness_position: Acting Branch Head, Data Centres Energy Taskforce

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The Clean Energy Investor Group and Baringa released analysis showing that data centres not covering their energy demand with new renewables will push up power prices by 26 per cent in New South Wales and 23 per cent in Victoria. Do you know what the price impact will be of allowing them to build renewables after they have already connected to the grid? Is that something that you're considering and that you've got any modelling on as part of this process?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: As we said earlier, those matters are under active cabinet consideration at the moment, so there's not much we can add.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
witness_position: Acting Branch Head, Data Centres Energy Taskforce

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not full of confidence with that response. There's no more information around—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There's no more information we can provide at the moment.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
witness_position: Acting Branch Head, Data Centres Energy Taskforce

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We've submitted two questions on notice, one to Treasury and one to your department, Minister, on diesel use forecasts. Based on your 2025 emissions projections report, you say that diesel use will decline by 1.5 billion litres by 2030. However, based on fuel excise in the budget papers, Treasury confirmed that we will be burning 2.4 billion litres more in 2030. So one department is saying diesel consumption will be increasing while another says it will be decreasing. Can you please provide some clarity?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not sure I'm in a position to provide much clarity. If there's any information that comes to me in the next few moments, I will do that; otherwise, if there's an official who's in a position to provide an answer, I'm very happy for them to do that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm so sorry, but I'm going to have to ask: could you please repeat that question, as we were just coming up to the table and didn't hear you?
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. We submitted two questions on notice, one to Treasury and one to the department, on diesel use forecasts. Based on the 2025 emissions project report, the department says that diesel use will decline by 1.5 billion litres by 2030. However, based on the fuel excise in the budget papers, Treasury confirmed that we will be burning 2.4 billion litres more in 2030. So one department is saying diesel consumption will be increasing while the other says it will be decreasing. I am just curious to know which one is correct.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I am not familiar with that exact question on notice. I don't think I have it in my pack, but I would say that our current best estimate of diesel consumption into the future is indeed in the 2025 emissions projections that you have cited and that our next, more updated assessment of that will be in the 2026 emissions projections, which are due to be tabled by the end of this year. Apologies, because it's like taking on notice a question on notice, but I would have to look at that discrepancy.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We can bring up the questions on notice and perhaps return to this later in the session. I'll save that question block until you've familiarised yourself.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: If we can do that, we will.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: To the department: the No. 1 complaint that we hear from the renewables sector is that there is no investment certainty, because Origin, the New South Wales government, the Victorian government and the Queensland government keep extending their coal fleets. Is this the feedback the department is hearing too?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We do hear that feedback. It is probably less than it was a few years ago. I think there's increasing certainty in the short term about the exit of coal-fired generators. Things become a bit more uncertain when you look at the generators scheduled for closure around 2035, but I think there's a greater sense of certainty in the industry now, for some of the generators that are slated for closure pre 2030, that the necessary investments in system strength have been made. I think AEMO's recent ESOO is evidence of that.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Would it be fair to say that the most recent spikes in the energy market are from coal outages and unplanned repairs?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I think it plays a key role. I think colleagues will have the exact figures, but out of 17 peak price days in 2025, eight of those were associated with unplanned coal exits. So it is playing a part in some of those peak price days that can have a big impact on household bills.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Are you worried that coal extensions are materially affecting the ability to reach 82 per cent renewables by 2030?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It is a key part of the equation but, as I said, those closures pre 2030 now appear to be more certain, based on the information that AEMO has published and based on my engagement with industry.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Do you expect the unplanned blackouts to increase?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I think they will continue to be a feature of the system, given the ageing nature of our coal-fired generators. They aren't getting any younger. Some of them are 50 years old. It will be a feature of the system until they're removed.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: This will presumably push up prices as well?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It will be a source of higher prices if they do continue to lead to unplanned outages.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: If the federal parliament set the time of coal closure in law, would this help spur investment in new generation?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I haven't really turned my mind to that. I think at the federal level our main focus is on driving investment in renewables and batteries, which we're seeing at the moment have an impact on prices, particularly in the shoulder period, which will make the coal-fired generators economically unviable.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But if states and Origin keep extending, this undermines the federal work, doesn't it?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It does. I think, though, the states have their own targets and they are keen to see a smooth transition, given some of the problems experienced with coal-fired generator outages. I've got no reason to believe they're not as keen to see those generators shut down on the scheduled timeframes as we are. They, just like us, want to make sure that the impacts on affordability and reliability are managed well. AEMO's latest report suggests that's all on track.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So you haven't considered at all federally legislating that? Minister, that's not something you've contemplated?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The way that this is delivered, we have our responsibilities at Commonwealth level and the states have theirs. There's a set of what I would see as pragmatic judgements being made about making sure that the capacity in the system that's required is there. Our job is principally providing the investment confidence in new generation and transmission and driving that process. At the end of the third quarter this year—so I guess that's last month—there were some 80.9 gigawatts of projects in progress through the connections process for the national electricity grid—80.9. There's a very substantial building process going on there. The destination is very clear. The faster we can build, the stronger the system. The faster we can build, the more industrial electricity jobs. We make room for new investments in metals processing. All sorts of opportunities are there, but in order to do that we need to build. So, when there are senators in this place who are opposing wind developments in regional areas, they are really opposing industrial jobs. There are senators and members of parliament who make wild claims in regional communities about these things. They are opposing blue-collar jobs, but our job is to get on with the build-out.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Minister, on the weekend it was reported that MAC Energy is saying the quiet part out loud in its annual reports. It's saying it's actively trying to influence curriculum and extracurricular activities. Are you aware of this?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I read that story with some interest. I guess my immediate reflection when I read that story was that, if kids in school in the Hunter Valley are filling out a colouring-in book that celebrates their mum or dad's work or their uncle or their auntie's work, there should be a bit less sneering at that, I reckon, from some of our broadsheets. These are communities where industrial work, whether it's in the new economy or in the old economy—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Would you say the same if they worked in tobacco or asbestos?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I guess I don't see an equivalency there. These are proud working-class people—proud working communities. I don't find—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You don't find it offensive to have these fossil fuel interests, who are often multinational corporations—purely profit driven—brainwashing our children and being in schools and educational facilities with their curriculum? They are purely profit driven. This isn't coming from a place of care and goodwill for the next generation.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We're talking about the work that people's mums and dads do.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We're talking about an industry that is ruining these young people's lives.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't think we advance the cause of more clean energy generation by denigrating the work of the people who work in those economies.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Big corporations.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The people! Don't forget the people.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not forgetting the people. They're the ones who need a just transition.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's my immediate reflection on that. I saw that as looking down on people.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Maybe to the department as well, as a last question: are you worried about this concerted effort by the industry to infiltrate our educational facilities and influencing kids as young as six months old? Do you think this has ongoing implications for our ability to combat the climate crisis?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't think that's a matter that we would offer an opinion on. We are interested as a department in information integrity and are playing an increasing role in that space as we seek to get quality information out there, but the educational efforts of various industries are not something that we would offer a view on.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: These aren't people selling vapes to kids, like the way that you've implied. These are good, honest Australians who are proud of their work driving big trucks and handling engineering work on big mines.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: If it was a tobacco, asbestos or gambling corporation, would you have the same response? People work in those industries.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't need a lecture about asbestos. Honestly, I've spent more time with workers who have worked for asbestos companies and are suffering from that. It's an utterly—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What about other people who are living in—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senators, once again, please don't talk over the top of each other. We will have questions and answers. I think, if I'm gauging that correctly, we've probably reached the fruitful end of that exchange. I'm going to move the call to Senator Ananda-Rajah.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I just have some questions regarding wholesale electricity prices and home batteries. How have wholesale electricity prices come down year on year in the last four quarters, and what has been the role of batteries and renewables in these outcomes?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We have seen in the National Electricity Market a significant decline in average wholesale prices. When we compare the September quarter this year with last year, there was a 27 per cent decline from the September quarter last year to this year. That has been attributed by the Australian Energy Market Operator to a range of factors. Certainly the increasing penetration into the market of both large-scale and small-scale batteries is playing a role. As I think we discussed earlier, that is, for example, reducing demand in peak periods, and that's flowing through to less gas generation, which tends to be higher cost and sets the market price in those peak periods. More generally, we have seen an increased amount of renewable energy in the market as well. Those are the sorts of factors that have led to that decline.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Do you have any data on how much less gas we are using?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not sure I have a specific figure on gas. Just the one figure here, perhaps: gas generation is down 34 per cent year on year and is now at levels that haven't been seen since the year 2000.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'll just add to Mr Archer's answer that the September Quarterly Energy Dynamics report that he referred to, released just last week, goes to show the change in the role that batteries are playing. In the third quarter of 2026, the daily average charged during the middle of the day was 13.4 gigawatt hours. Then it was discharging 10.9 of that back into the peaks, as Mr Archer said, driving down those peak prices that feed into household and small business bills. As a comparative figure to that 13.4 gigawatt hours, just 12 months ago that was 3.7. The 10.9 discharged into the peak 12 months ago was only 3.2. That's not only driving down the peaks; it means that, of the solar that was economically curtailed because of negative prices 12 months ago, almost half is now being fed into the grid and used. It's good for prices, but it's also good for us on progress to our renewable energy targets and in encouraging new investment.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So it's soaking up the excess solar during the day and then discharging it in the evenings and bringing down prices.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Exactly. It's taking it from when we have an excess and putting it to where it is needed, which is something we hoped to see, but we're now really seeing that at a level we didn't expect to see so quickly.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: How has the current default market offer helped to reduce retail prices? Could you please take us through what those results show, what this has meant for households and why this has occurred?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
The default market offer is set by the Australian Energy Regulator, and again we saw that decline for 2026-27. The rate of decline differed across the different NEM jurisdictions, and the AER attributed the lower DMO prices again to that role that batteries are playing but also to increased wind generation during evening peak periods, some reduced volatility in wholesale spot markets and lower wholesale electricity contract prices. The default market offer is reflected in the standing offers that retailers offer to customers. Probably around 8 per cent to 10 per cent of residential customers are on those standing offers, with the remainder being on what we refer to as market offers. Those are typically set at a discount to the standing offers. If the DMO is declining, you would expect market offers to also be reflecting that.

When we look at, for example, the information that the ACCC had in its NEM inquiry report, we're seeing quarterly electricity bills for residential customers—sorry, I have lost my train of thought.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It's good that this is the culture of this department: officials working together.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Continue. Don't worry.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Small businesses are also seeing price reductions. It differs across the jurisdictions, as Mr Archer said, but for New South Wales the price reduction is between 9 per cent and 11.3 per cent for flat rate small business customers, and 9.4 per cent to 20.9 per cent lower for time-of-use small business customers. In South-East Queensland, businesses are seeing prices 10.4 per cent lower for flat rate small business customers and 14 per cent lower for those who have adopted time-of-use charging. In South Australia, prices are 6.8 per cent lower for flat rate small business, and 12.1 per cent lower for time-of-use small business. Those are positive changes as a result of the greater use of wind and those batteries moving power from the middle of the day to the peak periods.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We might just go to EV uptake. EV sales are booming, as you know. Can you talk us through policies like the EV discount—I know we made some changes in the budget—and the new vehicle efficiency standard, what role these policies and others might be playing in spurring EV sales and also the impact on fuel consumption?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
I'll give you some higher level answers and some statistics that might be helpful, but if there's anything in particular that you would like us to go to beyond that we're not touching on, please let us know. It's been a period of rapid acceleration of uptake for electric vehicles across Australia, as has been well covered in the media. Uptake was already accelerating through last year but, particularly with the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East, it has rapidly accelerated, to the point where electric vehicles are accounting across the year for 28.6 per cent of new sales in Australia. That's the period from 1 January through to 30 September 2026. That's up from 13.1 per cent in the 2025 calendar year, so obviously those figures will shift a little bit more as we head to the end of the calendar year. On a monthly basis, in September 2026 alone, EVs accounted for 34.5 per cent of all light vehicle sales, compared to 16.1 per cent in September 2025. In both August and September of this year, battery electric vehicles—that's a specific subset of EVs—outsold petrol-only new light vehicles for the first time. So clearly a range of incentives are applying in the marketplace and Australian consumers are responding to that.

We attribute a lot of that to a combination of factors, but clearly there is a strong policy signal in there. I can't provide a particular breakdown of what proportion we think is due to, say, fuel prices versus policy signals, but clearly the new vehicle efficiency standard is having an effect. We can see that through a range of indirect outcomes in the marketplace, including a greater variety of electric vehicles on offer and a much greater range of vehicles at lower prices. My colleague Mr Ryan might wish to add some statistics to that.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: As Mr Hutchinson said, the number of EV models available in Australia has more than tripled over the last four years, from around 60 models in June 2022 to more than 230 models by October 2026. As of 1 October 2026, there are around 20 EV models with starting prices under $40,000.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
witness_position: Acting Branch Head, Land and Transport Branch

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I will now go to the coalition. Senator Henderson.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I want to turn to the Capacity Investment Scheme. Over all of the tender rounds to date, how many projects have been announced?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: One hundred and nine projects have been announced.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
witness_position: Branch Head, Capacity Investment Scheme Branch

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: How many of those projects have been contracted?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Forty-six have active contracts.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
witness_position: Branch Head, Capacity Investment Scheme Branch

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Could we have the list of both the announced projects and the contracted projects on notice? There are clearly many more announced projects than those which have been contracted. Why is that?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There are a few reasons. Some of them we are still negotiating with; we're still negotiating 36 contracts as of right now. There have been a number of projects that have withdrawn over time for various reasons. So 27 projects have withdrawn.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
witness_position: Branch Head, Capacity Investment Scheme Branch

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: They were 27 out of the 109 that are now not proceeding?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Talking in general terms, the projects that have withdrawn have done so for quite a number of reasons. There has been a material change in capital and construction costs for some of those projects. Some have had difficulty obtaining network connection or access rights to the network. There have been delays with planning and/or environmental approvals. Some have had difficulties securing power purchase agreements. Projects change their investment strategies sometimes as well. Projects may have withdrawn to seek other sorts of support, and at times ownership of those projects may change, which means they may no longer either wish to contract with us or be fit to contract with us.

witness_position: Branch Head, Capacity Investment Scheme Branch

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Some of those projects will proceed without the Capacity Investment Scheme and we also expect—and some have—rebid again into our tenders.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

text: It's a proponent driven scheme—in that proponents choose the technology and the location and then choose a level of financial support that they come to the Commonwealth with. Some of them will later reassess either the design of their scheme or the level of support—they haven't bid in enough support. So for a number of them the project hasn't collapsed; it's just that they can't meet the milestones we put in place for the level of support they have bid in. So they need to either rebid into a later CIS process or proceed without financial support or bid into one of the state schemes, like the New South Wales LTESA scheme.

text: I wrote to the Auditor-General earlier in October about a project they did in 2023 where they identified 127 relevant programs across 42 entities involved in climate, energy and the green economy. Would you be able to identify how many of those programs are in this department?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I also have questions around the transition of Australia's economy to net zero emissions by 2050. How many agencies within this department are involved in reporting on that transition of the Australian economy? The government has made projections around the size of the renewables and the green economy. I know that we track emissions and employment numbers and salary numbers for coalmines, for gas companies and for energy companies. What agency within this department, or what section within this department, is tracking jobs and salaries and value for the green economy?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Again, I think that goes to the first question you asked about the entities that this department is responsible for or that are in the portfolio, which we took on notice. More broadly, though, the government produces an annual statement and reports on that every year, and the next one will be coming out before the end of the parliamentary year. That is where we provide the most comprehensive update on what is happening across, I guess, the economy that's relevant to both the energy transition and climate change.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But what I'm trying to understand is who in the department is responsible for measuring and tracking that data.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In the department we do have a central policy area that looks at a number of indicators in terms of what is happening across the economy. Just as an example, we will look at and use data in terms of what's happening with the sales of EVs and what that looks like for EV charging.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Specifically, what I'm looking for is this: there's been a whole lot of commentary on the number of people employed in coalmining and gas. I've got analysis from the Treasury department of the decline of that industry. I'm just seeking to understand what data is being collected and managed, and by whom, on the number of jobs and the salaries that are being generated in the clean, green economy.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm thinking about my own department's work in this area. To the extent that this department's role is to essentially guide the development of a new electricity system, do future investments in critical minerals production that are electrified count as green jobs? I don't know.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Somebody should know, Minister, because you keep talking about it.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't think it's very useful. I think it's about new industrial jobs. I don't get too hung up on the pejorative labels for these things. I know others do.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Can I just keep this shorter, please, Minister? I'm an accountant by trade. If you can't manage it, you can't measure it. It's a bit of an age-old catchcry. This is a government that is driving the economy towards a new style of job and structural changes to our economy, but I'm seeking to find who is tracking this, who is measuring this and who can give me any data at all, because in the absence of that you can't measure it and you also can't assert it without data to support what you're seeking to do.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I think it's 1.4 million new jobs. Wages have gone up, and collective bargaining is stronger.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

text: My questions are about the New England Renewable Energy Zone. In the draft 2026 ISP, Integrated System Plan, the New England Renewable Energy Zone had only one stage, with a single 500-kilovolt double-circuit line listed as actionable and included in the optimal development path. Is that correct so far?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
There will be funding given by the federal government, so let's just focus on that. In appendix 5, the draft Integrated System Plan stated:

Ongoing analysis and stakeholder engagement between now and June 2026 is needed to ascertain whether the second stage will optimise benefits to consumers in the 2026 ISP.

Yet in the final 2026 Integrated System Plan, both stages, which included two 500-kilovolt double-circuit lines, were now anticipated as a single project. The final Integrated System Plan explained in appendix 5 that this was based on information provided by the New South Wales government. Minister, did AEMO, the Australian Energy Market Operator, conduct or have access to any analysis to determine whether proceeding immediately with both stages together was in the best interests of the consumer, as they promised?

text: I suppose what I would say is that one prominent local in that region said, 'We've made massive investments in the New England into renewable energy. He said in another interview, 'The federal government has delivered millions of dollars of investment already for renewable energy generation right here on our doorstep in places like Inverell and Glen Innes.' Mr Joyce said he's an enthusiastic proponent of renewable energy in New England. He said, 'In the long term, we understand that there may be a transition to other fuel sources and we've got to make sure that we're also part of that transition.' He also said, 'With other projects like the Sapphire Wind Farm going ahead, it also shows that the New England is leading the way in renewable energy production, and I will continue to advocate for the region as a growing power supplier for Australia.'

If that policy was lost, if it was put aside', Mr Joyce said, 'it would create huge uncertainty in the renewable market.' That was from Barnaby Joyce. 'We've got to make sure we stay consistent in that', Mr Joyce said, 'and because we need consistency, we need our colleagues in the Labor Party to come to a bipartisan position so that we can land this, so that we can create a mechanism that in the future we see the further construction of wind and solar and pumped hydro.'
