text: You've asked that several times. I think Mr Barnes has given you the answer he is able to give, and, as to the broader economic benefits of this project, that's already been outlined as well.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The revised NPV is very pivotal. So are you going to be releasing a new or revised NPV, Mr Barnes?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We'll take the provision of a business case, in whatever form, on notice.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But can I just ask: are you going to be releasing a new or revised NPV?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's a question for our board, and I'll take that on notice.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You would, as the CEO, be making a lot of these day-to-day decisions. Is it your plan to recommend to the board that there will be a revised or new NPV?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Our board has been focused on concluding the cost reassessment.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Hang on a minute. You can't even give us a guarantee about the NPV? Is it not reasonable that you would release a revised NPV?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We have been focused on the cost reassessment, and, obviously, the production of our annual report as our auditors review the impairment test for the organisation. I've given you some figures around the asset IRR, and I'll take on notice whether that can be provided in a subsequent advice.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Can I put this to you: I'm concerned that you're not releasing the NPV because your books—things don't add up, and the only way in which they add up is if you get a very substantial multibillion-dollar bailout from the government.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We signed off our accounts and published those last Friday with audit sign-off. I think I've described that we will need government support to complete this project.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But can I put to you that's why you are not giving us full and transparent information in relation to these very important financial benchmarks for this project?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And I'm sure that, when the support package is determined, there will be an accompanying narrative around the nature of that support package.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So can I assume that, when you say 'when the support package is determined', there will be a support package?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I've said that we've asked the government for support to complete this project.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Can I assume by your answer that the government has committed to you that it will provide some sort of support package?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The advice we provide to government is that we need support, and it's now with the government for consideration.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But you just said to me 'when that support package will be provided'.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Well, I'm making an assumption. I have not received that advice from the department's own minister.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So you haven't received any guarantee at this point?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No. We have received support to keep going on the project, which we received last year when we exceeded—when we said we were going to exceed the $12 million—

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And, if you don't receive that support, you will have a huge write-down before your eyes, won't you?

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The purpose of the support is to maintain our credit rating. It doesn't mean that you would necessarily be writing down the project unless you stopped the project.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Henderson, the minister has already said publicly that the government is now considering how best to support Snowy Hydro to deliver value for the taxpayer and bolster governance and oversight arrangements as the project progresses towards completion, and we'll make those announcements in due course.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Minister, $25 billion is not value for the taxpayer.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Well, if the original cost and project hadn't been worked out on the back of a beer coaster, we might not be having this conversation.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And Minister Bowen should not be in his job, because this is the most serious and significant blowout that we have seen in recent—

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Well, Mr Taylor—

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: living memory.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: holds a more senior position than he did when he was the energy minister who kicked this project off.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Australians are watching this, and they're laughing at how you continue to deflect. Twenty-five billion dollars, Minister—

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It was never going to cost $2 billion—

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: This is—

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: which is what Mr Turnbull and Mr Taylor came up with on the back of a beer coaster.

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Mr Bowen—

agency: Snowy Hydro Ltd

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. The way the ACCU scheme works is people register projects with us at the Clean Energy Regulator against methodology that has been approved by the Emissions Reduction Assurance Committee, and then they implement the project. Then, when they hit particular performance milestones, ACCUs are issued. Typically, if it was a landholder or the owner of a landfill, for example, they would contract with a carbon service provider, and typically the ACCUs are issued then to the project proponent. Those ACCUs are then generally shared between the carbon service provider and the project proponent, and that's a contractual matter between them. Your characterisation of in the order of 19 million ACCUs in the marketplace over the course of the last 12 months is correct. They can then choose how they sell those ACCUs. There are a wide range of options available to them. Some proponents choose to hold ACCUs for the future. Others will have sold ACCUs forward, typically to a safeguard entity, which will use them for compliance purposes, or they can sell them to an intermediary, who may be trading on the market

agency: Clean Energy Regulator

witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Can you give me some more information about the uptake. There's 587,000. Is that still going strong, or what's happening?

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, so 587,000 batteries, and we're running at a rate of about 8,000 applications per week. That demand has remained fairly steady since the adjustment to the incentive was made on 1 May. Collectively, across the 587,000 batteries, there's been 16.4 gigawatt hours of capacity added to the distributed system. We are starting to see the impact of that storage in the marketplace. As reported by AEMO and others, we've seen that the wholesale price at the end of the day in the peak period has begun to decline significantly, and that is a result of the combined effort of both domestic storage—that 16.4 gigawatts—and the utility storage, which is enabling sun to be captured in the middle of the day and then redistributed through battery storage to the end of the day where there is peak demand.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Are battery installations helping consumers who do not install batteries?

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
I would most certainly say yes, both in the near term and in the longer term. In the near term, what we are seeing is a significant reduction in those wholesale prices towards the end of the day. We, along with others, are very keenly watching to see those reductions in price be passed through to consumers. In the longer term, what battery storage does is it allows us to fully utilise the distribution networks that we have. In simple terms, that's the poles and wires that we have in and around our houses, and those systems can very quickly become overloaded. If those systems become overloaded, then more capital is needed to be invested by our distribution network service providers.

Battery storage enables us to use that existing suite of assets more effectively. That's going to be incredibly important because, as households electrify, they also consume more electricity. For example, they switch their hot water system from the gas to an electric pump system, and, of course, we're starting to see a very significant uptake of electric vehicles—all of which has seen a significant uplift in overall demand. We need to make sure that lift in demand from our households can actually be supported by the whole grid. Why this is important to the whole community and all households is that, if we have to build more infrastructure within our distribution systems, those costs are passed through the retail system to households. So wherever we can avoid capital costs, there is a benefit to all households.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: How is the solar rollout going across the country?

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm assuming that the battery program has helped drive the uptake of rooftop solar as well.

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. If you just bear with me for one moment. For the year to date, as of 30 September, we had 2.8 gigawatts of solar installed, and that rate is on track to be a record year. What we're seeing is with the advent of the Cheaper Home Batteries program, households are doing two things. The first is they're installing larger systems. Typically, four or five years ago, a system would have been in the order of five to six kilowatts. A typical system is now above 10 kilowatts, so the same number of households but more capacity. The second thing is we're seeing an increasing number of households. About 25 per cent of installations are from households that are replacing one of the original solar systems. These systems would typically have been very small. They might have had secured a significant feed-in tariff. That was very common at the time when these schemes first started. That feed-in tariff is now sunseted, or stopped. So they're choosing to move from, say, a 2 to 2½ kilowatt system to a 10 to 15 kilowatt system with storage.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What system do you have in place to ensure compliance with scheme requirements, and have you updated requirements to ensure better outcomes on issues such as labelling?

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We have very extensive systems to address those risks, and, frankly, it's been a major focus for me in the last few weeks coming on board to understand how the regulator has considered and sought to address the risks. Of course, there's an inspection program that's required to be a statistically significant number of systems inspected, but safety and consumer regulations also apply at both state and territory level and then through Commonwealth consumer protections. Would you like to talk in some detail, Mr Binning, about the way we are addressing those risks?

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The first thing I'd say is that the Cheaper Home Batteries program leverages the infrastructure that is in place for more than 10 years under the renewable energy target, and there are two absolutely core controls to ensure that the system is safe. Firstly, there is the product listing process, which is done through the Clean Energy Council. What that does is ensure that any batteries that are brought into the country comply with international standards. And that ensures that they have very specific protections in place that prevent overheating or prevent thermal runaway within the battery unit. In the time that we've been running the program, with more than 580,000 batteries, we have not had a single event that is directly associated with a battery. We have had one fire that has been associated with a wiring issue in Western Australia. That was thoroughly investigated and shown not to represent a systemic risk. This really stands in very sharp contrast to other lithium ion devices. I'm talking about scooters, vacuum cleaners, electric drills and other power tools. They quite often associated with fires.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
In Queensland, there were 300 fires in 2025-2026. In New South Wales, the latest data we have is 323 in 2024 and growing. The reason for this is that the standards are not as strong, and people will often make an error in the management of that device and the charging of it. In simple terms, they plug it into the wrong charger; it overheats and catches fire. So we're very comfortable that the products are safe.

The second control is associated with that all installers must be accredited, and, to be accredited, they must have done training and had that added to their electrical licence. This means that they understand how to do it properly. Finally, we've been doing additional testing of batteries, which is essentially buying them off the shelf. We've been sending them to the University of Queensland to be tested. Through our inspections program, 4½ thousand inspections have now been completed, and we have seen very low rates of unsafe installation. Those rates are less than one per cent. We meet with our state and territory colleagues' electrical regulators, and they are very comfortable with that core statistic.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: For those inspections that you're talking about, are they across every state and territory?

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. Our task is to undertake a statistically representative sample. That's across both the numbers and also across the geographic distribution. So it is across all states and territories. What we're seeing, though, in that inspection program is that we have got high rates of non-compliance with some of the very detailed technical requirements, and, Senator, you asked about labelling.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
Labelling is the most common technical non-compliance that we are observing. I would emphasise that in the vast majority of cases, labels are in place; they haven't just been placed in precisely the right location or have precisely the right wording associated with them. To address that, we have been running an education program through industry networks, Solar Accreditation Australia, the Smart Energy Council, the Clean Energy Council et cetera. We've introduced a new control which requires people to lodge photographs with us around the labelling requirements. And, finally, in the last few weeks, based on advice from the industry advisory implementation committee for the program, which is a cross-section of industry players, I've written to the state and territory electrical regulators, seeking a review of the labelling requirements. I think there are up to about a dozen different labels that are required. It's very complex. The feedback we're getting from industry is that it is extraordinarily difficult to comply with. We are also getting feedback that it's not leading to a safer outcome and it's not informing households. So we've written seeking a review of that process. In no way do we want to compromise, but we do want simple, clear warnings provided to industry.

So what I would say, just in summary is that we are very confident in our systems, but we in no way are complacent. The protection of households, safety and consumer protection are our highest priorities. We run assurance programs so that we can identify issues and we can continuously improve. The labelling is a very good example of that. We are working very hard with the industry to lift their performance, and, at the same time, we're seeking to simplify their requirements so that we get better outcomes for households.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Scheme Operations Division

agency: Clean Energy Regulator
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Clean Energy Regulator

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Murray Watt, Minister for the Environment and Water, and call officers from the department in relation to outcome 4, Improve the health of rivers and wetlands and enhance the sustainable, efficient and productive use of Australia's water resources. That's program 4.1, Protect, restore and sustainably manage Australia's water resources, including the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder and the Murray-Darling Basin Authority. I welcome the relevant officials to the table from those agencies, as well. Minister, do you have an opening statement?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
I do. It's pretty brief. Thank you, Chair, for the opportunity to provide an opening statement to the committee. We're obviously now moving into the environment and water part of this department. It's taking the collective efforts of governments, environmental organisations, scientists, researchers, philanthropists, industry and local communities to achieve meaningful steps towards restoring and protecting Australia's natural environment. There's a mountain of work being undertaken by the public servants in this room to deliver better outcomes for our lands, oceans, forests and rivers.

This year we've made great progress building on Australia's strong foundation of sustainable ocean management. This is being done by launching our Sustainable Ocean Plan, beginning work to expand our marine parks and ratifying the high seas biodiversity treaty to protect marine species in the high seas. Whether in our regions or urban communities, our government is committed to delivering healthier outcomes for our environment and for future generations through programs like the Urban Rivers and Catchments, Saving Native Species and Australian Bushland programs.

We're working steadfastly and collaboratively to protect Australia's unique plants and animals from threats like bird flu, invasive species, climate change, natural disasters and overdevelopment, and we're ensuring the frameworks that protect what's most precious are modern and fit for purpose through reforms to the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, cultural heritage laws, the Murray-Darling Basin Plan review, waste regulation and more.

Of course, my biggest priority remains the implementation of the Albanese government's historic reforms to the EPBC Act. This Saturday will mark 12 months since our government introduced a bill to make these reforms. These reforms passed the parliament last December and are already better protecting our environment while powering productivity through faster and clearer decision-making processes. Within the last financial year there's been a five per cent boost to the number of on-time decisions made under the EPBC Act. Ninety-three per cent of statutory decisions were made on time in that period, a far cry from when the former coalition government delivered just six per cent of project approvals on time. The Office of Impact Analysis noted potential median savings for businesses of between $3 billion and $7 billion per year based on reduced delays, duplication and regulatory costs. We haven't waited a day putting these laws to work, and all reforms will be enacted by the end of this year. A cornerstone of the reforms was the creation of Australia's first national Environmental Protection Agency on 1 July—a modern, transparent and accountable regulator. In the EPA's first 100 days, it gave the greenlight to 77 projects under the EPBC Act, including projects supporting housing, renewable energy and critical minerals. That includes another 17 housing projects in the past three months, delivering 6,600 new homes. The EPA, in that period of time, has also managed 15 ongoing criminal court matters, finalised a criminal prosecution and seized thousands of illegal wildlife specimens.

The EPA has also developed clearer and more transparent advice through the release of the Agriculture and the EPBC Act guide to help farmers, landholders and agricultural stakeholders understand their obligations. They've progressed the implementation of the next phase of environmental reforms, including preparations for the implementation of Australia's first national environmental standards and a streamlined assessment pathway commencing on 1 December. Of course, they're only just getting started. As you've heard, and, as I'm sure we'll canvass tonight, the Albanese government is delivering meaningful outcomes for Australia's environment while also speeding up decision-making. We look forward to answering your questions today.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

text: I welcome Dr Simon Banks, the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder, and Mr Andrew McConville, chief executive of the Murray-Darling Basin Authority, and ask if either of you wish to make an opening statement. If so, I'd ask it to be relatively brief.

text: No, I don't.

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Mr McConville?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In the first instance, I want to ask about environmental watering. Can environmental water that's owned by the Commonwealth be released onto private land without the landowner's consent?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No, it can't.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Are you aware of recent New South Wales legislation that has provided that state with the powers to release water onto private land?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What I understand is that the legislation was changed in New South Wales in relation to WaterNSW liability. That's not just about environmental water; it's about all water deliveries. At the end of the day, I think it's best if those sorts of questions are directed to the New South Wales government for them to provide commentary.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Did they consult with anyone else in the Australian government? Will the CEWR or any Commonwealth environmental water use these New South Wales regulations to deliver environmental outcomes?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: When we place an either, either through our delivery partner or directly using the licences that we hold, those water deliveries are delivered by the river operators. In the case of New South Wales, it's WaterNSW. It's their responsibility to make sure that the water is delivered according to their arrangements and the legislation that they operate under.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Given that we've established that those provisions now do allow water to be delivered onto people's land without their consent and that you use them as the delivery agency, won't Commonwealth environmental water now go onto people's land without their consent?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It will only go on the land as it's delivered by WaterNSW.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But they can do this. They can deliver water without landowners' consent now. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: They've got to work collaboratively with the community around how they use the water or manage the water deliveries within the river operating arrangements and rules that they operate under. These questions are best, in terms of how that applies in New South Wales—
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But it's your water. They're delivering our water that you've paid for—we've paid for—and the Commonwealth government owns. I go back to my first question. My first question was: do you deliver water onto people's land without their consent? Does that happen?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We don't directly deliver the water to people's land without their consent. When Commonwealth water, irrigation water or any other kind of water is delivered within the system, it's the river operator, like WaterNSW, who has responsibility for delivery.

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Can you guarantee that no Commonwealth held water ends up on someone's land without their consent?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I can't guarantee that because, again, our responsibility is placing an order, like any other licence holder within the regulated system, and then it's up to the river operator to meet that order. That applies whether it's Commonwealth water, our general security entitlements, or whether it's irrigation water, conveyance water or other water that's delivered.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But it is the policy not to do this. Your intent is not to deliver water without the landowner's consent. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's correct. But, again, what we do is place an order, and then the responsibility of the river operator is to meet that order, and they will do that in the legal framework that they operate within to deliver the water.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What steps have you taken since the passage of the New South Wales legislation to assure yourself that your policy will be implemented by the New South Wales government agencies and the delivery authorities you rely on to deliver environmental water?

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We've been working with WaterNSW and our delivery partner on a standard operating procedure, which is about how they give early warnings to people who live along the rivers. I can ask Dr Finn, who has been working more closely on that, to provide more details about the standard operating procedure. This is just an arrangement between us and—
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Is this being triggered by this legislation or is it a separate process?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It has, on the basis that WaterNSW have an obligation to manage the water in good faith to minimise impacts to landholders.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
Senator, as you mentioned, New South Wales did pass legislation last year associated with WaterNSW and their deliveries of water on private land. That's New South Wales legislation. As Dr Banks said, our understanding of the way the legislation works for WaterNSW is that it allows them to deliver water as they need to as a water delivery operator or river operator, but they do have to act in good faith with landholders when they seek to deliver along flow paths into wetlands and all those sorts of things.

So WaterNSW as an institution are going through a process of setting up this standard operating procedure with environmental water holders—not just us but also in New South Wales—to allow them to go through that good-faith process. The standard operating procedure we've been working on with them is still a draft and not yet finalised, but it covers off on a range of things, including environmental water holders like DCCEEW and New South Wales providing information on the delivery that we propose to do—things like potential flow rates at particular gauges, information that could be useful for landholders to understand what those flows look like. It also asks us to provide information—and we often do this in collaboration with New South Wales—on engagement that we've had with potentially affected landholders and also summaries of the views of those landholders. A lot of the information that is currently in the SOP allows WaterNSW to be in a position where they're assured that there has been significant information exchange and appropriate engagement. It also puts them in a position, when they do come to deliver those flows and fulfil those orders, where they can provide information to the broader community about what those flows might look like. So that's the process that we are going through with WaterNSW to allow them to demonstrate that they have acted in good faith with the people in the catchment where they're delivering water.
witness_position: Branch Head, Environmental Water (Northern and Central Basin) and Science

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Will any provision of the standard operating procedure require WaterNSW or any NSW government agencies to receive landowner consent before water is placed on their land?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Again, this is New South Wales legislation, but—
witness_position: Branch Head, Environmental Water (Northern and Central Basin) and Science

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

I'm interested in the implementation of what was hitherto the Commonwealth government's policy, which was not to put water on people's land without their consent. I don't care if it's the SOP or some other arrangement. They're a customer of yours. You're paying them—they're your agent. Are you going to demand from them that they do not put water on someone's land without their consent?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What we will do is work with WaterNSW. They've got—
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Can I get a clear answer to that question? Plenty of farmers here are very worried. This is their land. It's productive land. They paid for it. It's their asset. How would you feel if a government agency came and said, 'We're going to use a part of your block for a period of the year, and you've got no say over it'? You said at the start of this that this was your policy not to do this. Are you going to ask the New South Wales government not to impinge on someone's property rights and put water on their land without their consent?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We'll continue to deliver our water through WaterNSW or other river operators, consistent with the legal arrangements that are in place, which means that, in New South Wales, WaterNSW will deliver the water consistent with their legal obligations, and we, just like any other—
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What seems very clear to me, then, is that you're using WaterNSW not just to deliver your water; you're using it to subvert at least the Commonwealth government's policy here—if not, the constitutional requirements on the Australian government—not to take over someone's property without compensation.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No, Senator. We—
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You say you don't want to do this, that you don't want to put water on someone's land without their consent, but then you're going to wash your hands—excuse the pun—with water here and get WaterNSW to do your dirty work for you.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's what's happening here.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No, we work very closely—
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Clearly, it is.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: with landholders. We work through arrangements to deliver water to wetlands on their land. There will be places like the Gwydir, for example, where WaterNSW have their own obligations around delivery of water, and it's not just environmental—
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

We've had very good relationships with the landholders to avoid those instances as best as possible.
