agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
A specific assessment of that decision? The short answer would be, no. It's very difficult for us to determine all the commercial factors that go into a decision like that, noting that in 2019, and from 2007 to 2010, SunRice also mothballed processing facilities during dry periods of time. Obviously, water availability and climate are significant driving factors of those types of decisions.

The most recent bit of government analysis about SunRice and rice processing facilities was undertaken by ABARES in, I think, 2024. That was commissioned by the New South Wales government in the context of its decision to end the rice vesting arrangements in New South Wales—essentially to deregulate that industry in New South Wales. That produced a report that, as the minister said, pointed to a number of contributing factors that were affecting the decline in the rice crop and subsequent viability of maintaining the processing footprint as it had in the past, which included that vesting decision and, also, significant transfer of water use in the Riverina, which, historically, if you went back to the '90s would have been used for growing rice crops, but which has shifted to other crops in that part of the southern basin now. There's significant cotton growing. There's several cotton gins that have been built in the southern New South Wales Riverina in the last 10 years. So there is a structural adjustment that's occurred, over a number of years, in the rice industry. As the minister said, while, yes, water recovery and anything that reduces the availability of water are factors, I don't think you could solely attribute the decision to the 450 or recent water purchasing activity.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I just want to be clear, I'm not trying to be a Monday expert. I was in just a few months ago making this very point—that buying back water while it was dry and the temporary water price was $400 was just insane. What was the rush? Why did you have to make 216 gigalitres of purchases, earlier this year, at a time when the farmers were already under stress?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Because, many years ago, a target of 450 gigalitres was set, well before our government was elected, and, of course, only two gigalitres of that amount was recovered under the former coalition government. We have committed to deliver on that target, because we think that that's important for the long-term health of the basin environment, industries and communities. We need to get there. We're not going to put our heads in the sand, like we saw from the former government, only recovering two gigalitres. We've got a legislated target, to be met by the end of next year, of 450 gigalitres. That does involve ongoing recovery.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So the target is more important than people's jobs?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No. The target is important for people's jobs in the basin in the long term. If we continue to see water overallocated from the Murray-Darling Basin, as we have seen for decades, we are going to see the demise of many more jobs in the basin than what we've seen over the last few years. We don't want to condemn basin communities, the basin environment or basin industries to a certain death, which would occur if we continue over-allocating water. It was only in January this year that I accepted the expert advice that the lower Murray is critically endangered. Of course, the Rudd government listed the same area as critically endangered, and, of course, that was overturned by the Abbott government. We are not going to stick our heads in the sand about the long-term impacts of overallocation. We will continue to support industries in the basin—like we did at SunRice recently, in Leeton.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But, if the target is not more important than jobs, why didn't you factor in these job losses when deciding to push ahead with 216 gigalitres of water purchases?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We have factored in the fact that delivering the plan including voluntary water buybacks—again, I know the National Party only ever focuses on the water-buybacks part of the Murray-Darling Basin Plan—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Actually, we focus on people's jobs, and you refuse to—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No. Do you want to let me finish?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: but, okay, go on a political diatribe and ignore people's jobs—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No, it's not a political diatribe.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You just mentioned them; I haven't mentioned Labor—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm just inserting some facts. You might like to meet a few facts every now and then. The facts are that, in addition to water buybacks, this government has funded over $870 million in water infrastructure and water efficiency, so it's not only about buybacks. We have also acknowledged that, in undertaking the plan including buybacks, that will have impacts economically on some regions and some industries. That's why we are providing $300 million in structural adjustment funding, which includes the recent amount that we delivered via our co-investment with SunRice in Leeton.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You mentioned the original plan required 450 gigalitres. Did the original plan require a social and economic neutrality test for that recovery?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: My understanding is that it was, and this has been well traversed. Yes, last term, our government amended the legislation to remove that test. Socioeconomic factors are still taken into account.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Exactly. Originally, you were claiming that for this target your hands were tied, that the target was what it was, that it was enacted in law and that, as a minister, you've got to apply the law and you've got to deliver the 450 gigalitres. But you misled us there, Minister, because the original 450 gigalitres had, explicitly, a social and economic neutrality test which would have given you the power to avoid these job losses. And you just admitted that your government made a specific decision to remove the test—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We did that last term.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: and allow you to prioritise the target of a water recovery amount over people's lives and jobs. That's explicitly what your government decided.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't accept that that's what we've done—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You just said it. The tape will show that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: and that's not what I said. Last term, not this term, we made that decision. We stand by that decision. Whenever recommendations are made to me around voluntary water buybacks, one of the factors that is put forward for consideration is socioeconomic impacts. It is not binding on me. As I say, you might like to say that undertaking voluntary water buybacks loses jobs, but what will really lose jobs in the Murray-Darling Basin is continuing to ignore the reality of overallocation of water. We're not going to let that happen.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Canavan, I want to share the call.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'll just ask one more question. Did you receive any specific advice about the Leeton mill before agreeing to water buybacks earlier this year?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry, are you talking about the lost jobs at Deniliquin as opposed to Leeton?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Leeton and Deniliquin, yes.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't recall receiving advice specifically on those mills. But, as I say, we acknowledge in a general sense that the plan including voluntary water buybacks is going to have some job losses. What will have a hell of a lot more job losses is continuing to do what we've done for decades, which is overallocate water.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It's very Lord Farquaad. It's 'some of you will lose your jobs, but it's a sacrifice I'm willing to make'. That's what you're sitting there and saying. It's the modern Labor Party—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: If you want to come back—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: People's jobs, union jobs—doesn't matter.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'd be very happy to have this conversation with you down the track. If we continue down the path that your government did, all that will do is condemn those communities to a terrible future.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Other people have to sacrifice, not you.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We are providing financial assistance to encourage new industries. You just heard about developments in the cotton industry that are creating jobs. So, yes, there are some jobs being lost. When those Deniliquin jobs were lost, I said, 'No-one wants to see any jobs lost.' We've also seen jobs created. We will lose so many more jobs if we continue to ignore the fact that the Murray-Darling Basin is drying as a result of climate change—something, again, I know you have trouble with—and I'm not going to do that. I'm going to make sure that those basin communities are alive for a long time to come.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Thorpe.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'll talk about the stolen water on stolen land. In 2023, as the restoring our rivers bill passed, your government committed $20 million for a First Nations centred and led cultural flows planning program—some rations. Grant decisions for this purpose have just been published in August of this year. This has been three years in the making. Why the delay?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I might get the officials to talk about the detail of that program.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Walawaani njindiwan. I'm a very proud Walbunja Aboriginal woman, and I head up the First Nations Water branch in the department. It was announced in 2023, but we took the time to engage and consult with basin nations about the types of things that they would like to see be available through that cultural flows program and to set the parameters within the grant operating guidelines.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's great. Are the grants resourcing every nation in the basin?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: No, only those that were able to apply at that time. One of the things that we are doing at the moment is producing a series of toolkit measures. Those nations who weren't yet ready or able to apply at the time will be given resources to be able to do the same type of work.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Which nations have not been funded?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There have been over 50 nations that have been funded in the basin. I could provide a list on notice about who they are, and that would then let you know which ones haven't been funded.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Why have some nations been selected to progress their aspirations and not others?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: This grant program was a non-competitive grant, which meant that any nation that applied for the grant wasn't competing against another. As long as they met the guideline requirements, they would receive the funding.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It was $19 million of the allocated $20 million?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, about $19.4 million.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Why is there a $1 million shortfall?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Only those 50 nations applied, and there was a limit up to $300,000 per nation. Not all nations applied for $300,000. They applied for funding based on the work that they wanted to undertake through that grant program. So there is that remainder of $600,000 from that $20 million allocation.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The grants are just for a two-year timeframe. Will you commit to—I suppose it's for the minister—ongoing funding for basin First Nations and their representative bodies to engage on water related matters, as proposed by MLDRIN, the Murray-Darling Conservation Alliance and others?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Obviously that's subject to future budget decisions, but, certainly, as a principle, we want to continue lifting First Nations engagement in these issues.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Once projects are completed, how will you ensure cultural flows are delivered so that water can reach the rivers and First Peoples communities that need it?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I can answer that. We also have, in the Murray-Darling Basin, the Aboriginal water entitlements program, and that's that $100 million program where we are purchasing water across the basin. That water stays within the consumptive pool. We're in the process of undertaking further consultation on the enduring holding model for that $100 million worth of water entitlements. Whilst we're not determining how that body will implement or manage its water portfolio, one of the things that we would hope would happen is that those folks and nations that have put their cultural flows plans together would be part of that process for allocating or assessing that $100 million worth of water entitlements. We see a link between the two.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: One of the grantees receiving the highest amount, granted with $2.4 million, is First Nature Group Pty Ltd, a First Peoples owned environmental consultancy that was appointed by eight participating nations to coordinate the grant on their behalf. Seven of these nations do not have access to any of the grant funding intended to support them to develop their cultural flows management plans during the seven months since the grant commenced. You know this, do you?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I do.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So you obviously know about the First Nature Group. Are you aware that they changed key delivery arrangements with consultation and are withholding grant funding and no longer communicating with these seven nations?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We have been approached by those seven nations separately. They've also approached the grants hub, who are the contractors on behalf of the Commonwealth with First Nature Group, FNG. Because we are not the contractors, we are reliant upon the grants hub to be that investigator and liaise with FNG about the matters that have been raised by the seven out of eight groups. I know that the grants hub has written out to FNG requesting certain responses to the allegations that have been put forward. We're in the process now of the due diligence assessment going through from the grants hub to consider what has been raised through those allegations.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm aware that formal communications requesting an expenditure freeze and establishment of an alternative delivery mechanism through novation replacing an existing contract with a new one in consultation with the department and the Business Grants Hub have not yielded any resolution. Can you tell me why and what you are doing to address this.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The Business Grants Hub will look at various ways in which grants can proceed through that due diligence assessment process that they're undertaking. Novation is one of the pathways. There are some voluntary processes that can be undertaken, but in all of this FNG is afforded the right to respond to questions from that contractual relationship process. That's the process that's going through now. It'd be premature to assume what the outcome of that's going to be, because its current.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So First Nature Group has not responded to the request for novation or communicated in any way with the nations, and the Business Grants Hub has not provided any advice on next steps. The department has stated that it cannot become involved in the contractual relationship between the Business Grants Hub and First Nature Group. The result is a continuing stalemate with nothing happening to address this governance failure while these nations whose work the grant was established to support remain unable to access funding or progress for the project. Do you agree that this is not in line with the principle of free, prior and informed consent? You would know that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I would know about FPIC, and I encourage that all the time, as do you. I really want to acknowledge that there is a deep sense of frustration with the process at the moment, because it does take time. But I am encouraging you, who you're representing and who has raised this with you. We do need to go through that due diligence assessment process because at the end of the day it will get a better outcome than shortcutting processes. I do again acknowledge that it is frustrating for those seven nations—very much so.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. Minister, on 5 October 2026, the consortium of these seven basin First Nations wrote to you directly about these issues and requested a meeting by 14 October. Have you responded to that letter? Have you met with them? If not, why not?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't recall having seen that letter myself. I don't recall having replied to it. Many of the letters that I receive are replied to by someone other than me. I receive a lot of letters. I don't believe I've met any group about this specific issue. I heard you refer to MLDRIN a little earlier, and as you probably know I did meet with MLDRIN some time ago—not necessarily about this specific issue, but I'll ask my staff to see where that correspondence is up to.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Great. Would you meet with them?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'd want to understand exactly what the issue is first, but I'll certainly ensure that either I or another appropriate person meets with them.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I just said what the issue was.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I know. I've heard your description of it. I'd like to get some advice on that as well. Again, I try to meet everyone I possibly can, but there are more people who seek a meeting with me than I can possibly meet myself.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: These are blackfellas. These are people of the land, of the water. It's respect.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I meet with First Nations people pretty regularly.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I know who you meet with.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I do meet with First Nations people.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I know who you meet with.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And I've met with MLDRIN.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I know who's given you the bad advice too.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I met with you recently.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. Let's talk about Djab Wurrung trees. You're going to protect those ancient birthing trees, over 800 years old, older than the colony itself?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not having a go here: this is the one your family's—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It's Djab Wurrung. Yes, that's my bloodline connection, and we've been fighting a road being widened. It takes six minutes off the freight trucks that drive really fast, and they need to wipe out a very sacred women's area. We've put a section 18 in, so I'm just wondering where that's at, because people have been arrested. We had 40 riot cop cars rock up last week. They've arrested Djab Wurrung women, mothers, grandmothers—quite violent. This has been going on for years—10 years or eight years.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. When we get to the next outcome, with the EPA, they would be better placed to tell you what's being done about that particular issue, because they're the regulator. This is the water people within the department. But I am happy to get the relevant—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It's been sent to you, though.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But, yes, I understand. In 2023, your government also committed $60 million for the Aboriginal Water Entitlements Program because I was in balance of power. You got a vote from me to get that money for my people, and this was allowing First Nations in the Murray-Darling Basin to purchase water entitlements for self-determined use. How much water is owned? It's all ours, stolen, but how much water is owned from the colonies allowing us First Nations people to have, as a result of this, this $100 million so far?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'll get the officials to give you the exact figure, but 'it's not as much as it should be' would also be my answer.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Well, you're the minister. You can sign it off.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And that's why we're funding this program.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Give it all back.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Why don't I get Ms Hedges to give you the answer?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: As of 18 September, we've exchanged 50 contracts for 21.5 gigs—or megs, I should say, not gigs. That would be extraordinary. That's just shy of $84 million worth. We're on track by the end of the year, December, to have committed or contracted up to that $100 million amount. At the moment it's held by the Commonwealth, but we are working under an interim governance arrangement, which is independent First Nations people from the basin who've been appointed in an advisory role and the directorate role to make those commercial decisions and to have in place those policies that are culturally led policies for how that water is purchased from there.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I have just one more. Who manages the water that's been purchased, and what proportion of the water purchased for First Nations is being managed by First Nations?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It's held by the Commonwealth at the moment, but we have a directorate in place which has three directors on it, and two associate directors in a mentoring role. Four of those are independently recruited from basin First Nations to do the directorate role. I'm the chair of that because of the fiduciary requirements from the Commonwealth perspective. When we're making those directorate positions, we do it with a fiduciary hat on. So, at the moment, we hold that. At some stage, we will be looking to work towards a trading policy for that, because part of the portfolio purchases was based on connectivity and wealth creation, and that will be managed until such time as the enduring model is established and held by First Nations people.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you for appearing tonight. These questions should have pretty short answers. Has the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder undertaken any assessment of the extent to which Commonwealth environmental water holdings may affect Australia's capacity to maintain essential agricultural production and domestic food security given the rapid growth in our domestic population and the need for agriculture to take a larger share of our exports to compensate for reduced manufacturing?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you for your question. I see Mr Coates has come to the table as well. What we've got is a set of figures that compares the gross value of irrigated agriculture production in 2005-06 to 2020-21. That was a slight increase from $9 billion in 2005-06 to $9.8 billion in 2020-21. That's GVIAP in the Murray-Darling Basin. Nationally, for example, the gross value of agriculture, fisheries and forestry production increased by 45 per cent in the past 20 years in real terms, from $69.3 billion in 2004-05 to $100.3 billion in 2024-25.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: They're actual figures. Have you done any modelling of the trade-offs?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I can ask Mr Coates to talk about the modelling we did prior to the purchase of the 450.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, we have done modelling of the impacts on agricultural production of the water purchases towards the 450 gigalitres. For the 300 gigs that has been approved for voluntary water purchase, the modelled impact of that is an impact of $122 million per annum worth of agricultural production, off a baseline of around $7 billion per annum in the Murray-Darling Basin itself, so it's about 1.8 per cent of irrigated production there. As my colleague made the point, nationally, total agricultural production is hovering around that $100 billion mark. This question was discussed at the Senate inquiry into the 2023 legislation, and the advice of officials from the department of agriculture at that time was that the scale of impacts from this marginal water purchase was not such that it would give rise to any concerns about impacts on food security or prices.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: What about rising population and falling manufacturing?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I think Australia is and remains a country with a substantial surplus of production, and we export around 70 per cent of our domestic agricultural production. The department of agriculture, again, is leading that work on Australia's food security strategy, and the discussion paper that they released on that—I think last year—led with the comment that the position of the agriculture department is that Australia is a food-secure nation.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. Has the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder modelled the interaction between its environmental water holdings and water availability for irrigated agriculture under prolonged drought scenarios?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In terms of the interaction between those modelling results and drought scenarios, we have, again, commissioned ABARES to do modelling of impacts of reductions in water supply in different climate sequences. That modelling, again, confirms that the overriding driver of changes in water prices and flow-on impacts is water availability. So, yes, impacts will be greater if water is less available.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You've modelled climate variability and cyclical variability?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The scenarios that we asked ABARES to model were not full climate sequences but just a simple quintile analysis of what it looks like in the wettest 25 per cent of years, in the middle and in the driest. They've produced a report that sets out those figures, which we could provide for you.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. Has it assessed the potential impact on agricultural production of reduced consumptive water availability during periods of severe scarcity?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I think that's the same severe scarcity as in extreme drought—the same basic set of parameters. I'd point you to the same report.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Excess going to the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm sorry, I'm just talking about water recovery under the Basin Plan, which ultimately does find its way, of course, to the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder, but this is within the water recovery targets set out in the Basin Plan and nothing beyond that.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. Has the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder consulted with the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry or Treasury about the economic and food security implications of environmental water management?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I've got to say, it's probably not within the remit of the environmental water holder, but the department has certainly consulted with the agriculture department on that. And, as I say, they provided evidence at the Senate inquiry into the Restoring Our Rivers amendments in 2023.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. Has any assessment identified circumstances in which the management or temporary trading of environmental water allocations could reduce risks to essential agricultural production while maintaining critical environmental outcomes?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not familiar with any modelling of that nature.
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Or any assessment?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: This is about changing rules around access to—
witness_position: Branch Head, Economics, Evidence and Engagement

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You recently announced a temporary trade of 15 gigalitres in the Gwydir.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: As the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder, I can offer some perspectives on that. Trade is an option, in terms of my responsibilities. The core focus of management of the Commonwealth's portfolio of environmental water is to protect and restore the environmental assets of the Murray-Darling Basin, and that's what we're focused on. Have we done modelling of what that looks like from a production perspective? No, we haven't. Our core focus is on returning that water to the environment. We've got really good evidence, through over 15 years of science, that demonstrates exactly what can be achieved through carefully planned and adaptively managed water, as the season unfolds.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Have you got a report illustrating or detailing that work?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The most recent report we have on our website is a basin-wide evaluation. That considers the environmental outcomes that we've achieved from the management of water. The most recent year that that's available for is 2024-25, and that's because it does take some time, at the end of the water year, to go through and do the analysis of the results to understand and attribute the outcomes to the use of the Commonwealth's water. But that certainly demonstrates and provides evidence of the outcomes that we can achieve.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: This is not me being cheeky, but does it also include evidence of and reports on the excesses of water that have caused harm to the environment?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In terms of excess that causes harm to the environment—we use the water to protect and restore the environmental assets, not to cause harm to the environment. Again, I think what we've been able to demonstrate through the management and the planning is that, as the season unfolds, we adaptively manage the water to make sure that we're contributing to positive outcomes. That might be supporting waterbird breeding or providing habitat for waterbirds. It can be to support the movement or breeding of native fish. It can be building resilience of our internationally important Ramsar wetlands. And we've got evidence that really shows that those sites that have received environmental water on a more regular basis are in a much healthier condition going into a drought and also coming out of droughts.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. Following on from the Gwydir Valley temporary trade of 15 gigalitres, will the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder consider further temporary trading of environment water allocations to reduce risk to essential agricultural production for Australia's future food security?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We've got a range of tools available. That's delivery of the water within the year to achieve environmental outcomes. We think about our carry-over, and, again, that's water that we can use next year to achieve environmental outcomes. And then, as you refer to, on trade, I can basically sell temporary allocations or annual allocations to also achieve environmental outcomes. In terms of the Gwydir, we basically look to sell up to 15 gigalitres of water. An important part of our transparency around our trade activities is that I'll update our trade intentions on a quarterly basis, we'll consider a range of factors in updating those trade intentions, and there will be notification when they're updated and publicly announced. That's our notification to the market of the intentions over the next quarter. And then we go into a process of further understanding and detailing the opportunities for trade in places where we've identified we're considering trade, through our trade intentions.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Just a minor addition to that: will the—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts, this will have to be close to your last. Then we will go to a short break and then we'll finish off water.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Will CEWH be looking to review their water trading process to adapt to agricultural planting windows?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: My focus is about protecting and restoring the environmental assets of the Murray-Darling Basin. Trade is a tool that we can utilise to achieve environmental outcomes, and that's on the basis that the proceeds of trade can be invested in environmental activities or projects that basically support the long-term outcomes that we are trying to achieve with the environmental water.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: But, if you're going to sell it, can you sell it at the best time for farmers?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: All those considerations, in terms of the trade intentions—there are market considerations. The primary is environmental. What are the environmental demands at any particular time? What do we need, in terms of water, perhaps, for the next water year? So we're thinking about our carryover. Then, obviously, we're thinking about, from a value-for-money perspective, what's the best opportunity in terms of potentially selling allocations? They're all considerations that go into the mix. Then what I'll do is notify the water market, through our trade intentions, of what we are considering. Our trade intentions at the moment are considering trade in the Gwydir, the Goulburn and the Namoi catchments. We're currently in the process, right now, of updating those trade intentions, and when that's publicly available we'll publish that on the website.
witness_position: Head of Division and Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We will take a very short break now, which will be by way of a comfort stop rather than a tea-break. When we come back we will go to Senator Pocock in outcome 4.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It's my privilege to say that we will let the Inspector-General of Water Compliance go, with the committee's thanks. I thank my colleagues for their cooperation in that respect, and we thank the inspector-general and his staff for all the work that goes into preparing for Senate estimates. We appreciate it, and you go with the committee's. I'll now go to Senator Pocock.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I've got some more questions about our favourite acronym, the SWIOID, and the review and its implementation. I'm hoping some of you may have seen the exchange earlier with Snowy Hydro. The department's website confirms that the independent review panel provided its final report to the Australian government in August. On what exact date was it received?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I can take that. The department itself received the report on 1 September.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So it wasn't in August.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I think the report was finished literally on 31 August. We received it the next day.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And which Commonwealth ministers have received the final report?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We've worked with our Energy colleagues to provide briefing material to ministers who look after water and energy, but that is still a work in progress.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So who's got it so far?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We have worked with our Energy colleagues to provide briefing material to the minister for water and the minister for energy, and the government is still considering that report. It's still early days.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: It also relates to the shareholder ministers, so it's also the Minister for Finance as a shareholder minister. We're in a position where we're not only actively briefing Minister Watt but working across with our Energy colleagues in terms of the shareholder ministers.
witness_organisation: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Have any of the three ministers asked for further information?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The three ministers—myself, Minister Bowen and Minister Gallagher—were verbally briefed by the review panel roughly a month ago or six weeks ago. I know that my department has been preparing advice for me since that point in time. I'm not entirely sure what further information has been sought by the other ministers or been provided to them.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's good to know. So what's stopping the report from being released?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In the scheme of things, the final report hasn't been with government for terribly long, and, obviously, we're wanting to fully consider the recommendations. It would be my intention to publish the final report, but we obviously want to give it a bit of further consideration before we do that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Given that there are shareholder ministers, it's your decision to release the report?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I think that's right.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's correct. The three ministers are relevant to the release of the report because it has an impact in terms of Snowy Hydro as well.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So all three have to approve that?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's the intent.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And how much longer before the advice from DCCEEW is to be delivered?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry; can I correct that last piece of evidence? The minister for energy and the minister for water are the two relevant ministers who have to agree to the content of that. But there's a whole-of-government consideration involved as well. And, as Mr Sullivan said, the finance minister is relevant as a shareholder minister.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And how much longer before that advice from DCCEEW is delivered to the minister?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: My office has actually just let me know—and so I believe—that advice has now been provided. I haven't seen that yet myself. I'm not having a go at my office; they need a bit of time to look at it as well.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: If I can just add to that, the department has been working through the content of that report to be able to provide comprehensive advice to all of the relevant ministers. We've sought to provide a whole-of-portfolio view because of the importance of the environmental outcomes for the river as well as the energy considerations.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I appreciate all of your work on it. It's a really important piece of work, and I look forward to seeing what the government's response is. Thank you.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Senator McLachlan.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I want to take us to the lower Murray and the Coorong lakes. They are critically endangered. What is the assessment at the moment of the health of the river system there, and has there been any improvement?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm sure there are some officials who are here now who could speak to that. As far as I'm aware, the intention is still to call the Threatened Species Commissioner, I think, later tonight, who would be able to speak to that work as well. We'll see who we've got here and whether they're able to speak to that.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I guess what you're also alluding to are the initial Sustainable Diversion Limit assessments, which were released in February and have been updated.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Well—

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I'm pre-empting a further question.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You anticipated my next question, which is about the considerable community angst about the shortfall. My next question was going to be towards understanding what your view was of the health. And then it was this: are their concerns justified, given there's a shortfall, and where do we go from here? That's basically three questions.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In short, as you know, in January this year, on the recommendation of the Threatened Species Scientific Committee, I did list the lower Murray as critically endangered. To my knowledge, there has been no update to any of that. But what that showed comprehensively was that the lower Murray remains in very significant environmental distress. I won't speak for the officials, but I think it would be fair to say that, were we to abandon key elements of the Murray-Darling Basin Plan, including voluntary water buybacks, that would not be a good thing for the lower Murray, given its very poor environmental state.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In relation to the health of the Coorong, Lower Lakes and Murray Mouth, the end of system, what we've seen over the last 15 years with Basin Plan implementation is that, essentially, it's a mixed story. We've seen significant improvement in the health of the Lower Lakes since the millennium drought, and the Basin Plan has been instrumental to that recovery. But, when we look further downstream, for the Coorong, we have not seen the same levels of recovery. The north lagoon of the Coorong has exhibited some improvement in health since the millennium drought, and, again, the Basin Plan has been instrumental to that. But what we're seeing in the south lagoon is that it is a degraded part of the system. It continues to remain degraded since the millennium drought. We're seeing that all components of the ecosystem are impacted in the south lagoon. And what our work under the SDL assessment is showing is that we do not have confidence that we'll be meeting the environmental targets that we've set for the south lagoon of the Coorong into the future.
witness_position: General Manager, Basin Science and Knowledge

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Where is that modelling held—the assessment of, 'If you don't get this much, this degree of degrading occurs'? The minister has drawn the nexus. Where is the flesh to that?

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In February this year, we released our initial SDL assessments, and we released a lot of modelling alongside that. We're currently in the process of working through the final SDL assessments that will appear as part of the Basin plan review final report. When the Basin plan review final report and the final SDL assessments are released, we'll release the evidence base at the same time. That will include the modelling. But the general trend of where we're heading, for the final SDL assessments for the South Australian Murray, looks quite similar to what the initial SDL assessment said.
witness_position: General Manager, Basin Science and Knowledge

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. At the moment, on the initial targets that we have for environmental flows, you're saying, to our best knowledge, they should be able to assist with the problems in the Lower Lakes. We're not going to find later we need more—well, we may, given climate change. But, at the moment, the targets are sound, as far as the current modelling holds.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That's right, yes. We have seen, through Basin Plan implementation, that Lower Lakes levels have been maintained within the desired range. Our modelling gives us confidence that we should expect to see that continue over the life of the next Basin Plan. But where the risk is most manifest is in the Coorong.
witness_position: General Manager, Basin Science and Knowledge

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thus the need to as quickly as possible find the environmental flows.

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Environmental flows—freshwater inflows into the Coorong—are the primary driver of health of the Coorong system.
witness_position: General Manager, Basin Science and Knowledge

agency: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. No further questions.

Program 2.2 is protect Australia's cultural, historic and First Nations Heritage, and program 2.3 is accelerate the transition to a circular economy while safely managing pollutants and hazardous substances.

I'll give you a couple of different figures. Since May 2022, when our government was first elected, 111 housing projects have been approved, which involves 85,000 homes. Since the commencement of the National EPA, on 1 July this year, 17 housing projects have been approved, which equates to 6,585 homes. We are approving 43 per cent of housing projects in as little as four to six weeks.

To come to the numbers you are asking about. As of 23 October this year, there are 15,727 homes, or 28 housing projects that are, if you like, with the National EPA—as in the ball is in their court. They're either awaiting an approval decision, awaiting a referral decision or, more generally, with the EPA for review. agency: National Environmental Protection Authority

text: No. I said to you earlier that we are approving 43 per cent of housing projects in as little as four to six weeks. So 43 per cent of housing projects get a very quick approval. There are others that are likely to have a significant impact on the environment. They are the ones that require an assessment. And if you'd like to know more about the major reason that they're under assessment, Mr Bradley can help you.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: If Mr Bradley can tell us that, we'll be happy.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: There are reasons why projects can take longer to progress through the system.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Just the top two.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The timeframes can be extended for a number of reasons, which are often not within the department's control. Some proponents choose to put their project into the system early while they're still working through some state and territory planning or zoning processes. Some are waiting for suburb infrastructure planning and construction, such as the development of roads and water supply, to be finalised before they progress their assessment, and some are considering a range of offset options. But if I look at the period in the last four years, there have been 81,000 homes that have been approved in that period of time, and almost half of those in the last 12 months. So we are, through the work that's been done around that housing strike force, increasing the pace.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So what are the top two?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The top two would be proponents that put their project into the system while they're still working through state and territory planning or zoning processes, or they're waiting for suburb infrastructure planning and construction. So, the kind of headworks to support the project.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: That sounds like a paperwork thing.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: In some cases it's an important part of enabling housing, which are the services that need to support housing projects like roads and water supply. The proponent is often working through those state level planning programs and securing the headworks with major utility providers.

text: Well, I make very few approval decisions. The overwhelming number, and I mean over 90 per cent, of approval decisions are made by a delegate.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Do you delegate?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. That's been the custom and practice for ministers—

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Are they published?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The EPA can correct me if I get this wrong, but, to my knowledge, every approval decision that is made, whether it be by the minister of the day or now the EPA is published. If that's not correct—

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And the decisions are fine.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: So you publish your decision, but why don't you publish yours?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I do. It's just that I make very few.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Do you publish all of yours?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: For example, I made the decision around the North West Shelf project last year.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, I remember that one.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I haven't made many others since then. As I say, for many years now, well over 90 per cent of decisions have been made by the delegate of the Minister, which used to be a departmental official. Now that we have the EPA, it's an EPA official, and they're all published.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: And how many housing ones have you made?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: I don't recall making any myself. I mean, there is a view amongst some that ministers should be making all the decisions or a significant number of them. My argument is that's a very good way to ensure that no decisions get made, because there are hundreds of decisions being made on a regular basis, and having a delegate at the EPA is an efficient way to ensure that decisions are still getting made and not sitting in a minister's inbox.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The average time for a resourcing project to go through?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You published that?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. I don't recall having made any others. If there are others that I've made, I'll let you know.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. The question is: how long does it take to get a resources project approved under EPBC in Australia?

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: While the officials are looking for some figures—some are made quickly, and some are made over a much longer period of time. That will depend on the complexity of the project, the significance of its environmental impacts and the responsiveness of the proponent.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: We have KPIs for decisions to be made within statutory timeframes. To give you an example of that, last financial year 93 per cent of all decisions were made on time. For the current financial year to 30 September, 93 per cent of project approvals were completed within the statutory timeframe. And I have to remind you that it got as bad as six per cent under the former coalition government in 2018-19.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: You've been in government for a long time now.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: The amendments, you might remember me saying, had three pillars. portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority

text: That is the case. Mr Bradley, I appreciate that you have been brought forward in unorthodox circumstances. I would ask you, very respectfully, to keep your opening statement as brief as possible, but, yes, if you'd like to make a short opening statement, please do so.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text:
Thanks very much. I appreciate it, Chair. Thank you for the opportunity to be with you today. Today is the first Senate estimates hearing for the National Environmental Protection Agency, and I want to begin by acknowledging the traditional owners of the land that we're on today, the Ngunnawal people. I pay my respects to their elders past and present and extend that respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples participating in the proceedings.

As the committee is very aware tonight, the agency was established on 1 July as part of those reforms designed to achieve the three broad objectives that the minister just discussed. In establishing the National EPA, we've consolidated a single environmental regulator with a national footprint. The team has diverse expertise and experience across 10 national environmental laws governing environmental assessments and approvals, wildlife trade, waste and recycling, ozone protection and contamination. As an independent regulator, our focus will be on ensuring compliance with Australia's national environmental laws, promoting best-practice regulation and helping to safeguard matters of national environmental significance for current and future generations.

Our initial focus to date has been on connecting to stakeholders and establishing our mandate, our critical business systems and our cultural priorities. Just as importantly, we're maintaining our momentum in critical responsibilities that protect environmental outcomes and economic activity. The minister has recently released a statement of expectations for the National EPA, and in coming months we'll publish a range of documents which will include our statement of intent in response and our first corporate plan, and we've recently published our regulatory posture statement. Thank you very much for the time with you tonight.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you, Mr Bradley. I appreciate the brevity of that statement. Senator Faruqi.

agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
portfolio: CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY, THE ENVIRONMENT AND WATER PORTFOLIO
text: Minister, I have a few questions on trophy hunting. I find it pretty astounding that, in 2026, we're still legally importing trophy hunted polar bears, American black bears, brown bears, giraffes, grey wolves, hippopotamuses, wildcats and many more. I just want to give a few examples of what has been imported here as trophies in the past two years: vervet monkey scrotum shot glasses, 13 hippopotamus teeth with a skull as part of a coffee table with hippopotamus feet turned into book stands, a rifle bag made of giraffe and a polar bear trophy. Minister, do you think it is acceptable to import these items obtained through trophy hunting to Australia? It makes sense they'd have to do that, right? Because we have a 'polluter pays' principle in this country. They're the polluter, so they should pay for such a program to seek to avoid the extinction of the Maugean skate, and these fish-farming corporations make hundreds of millions of dollars profit a year. agency: National Environmental Protection Authority
